questions.prompt: Explain why atoms of the same element can have different mass numbers. (3)
hints: Mass number counts protons and neutrons.
questions.solution:
Atoms of the same element have the same number of protons. [B1]
They can have different numbers of neutrons. [B1]
Atoms with the same proton number but different neutron numbers are isotopes, so their mass numbers differ. [B1]

questions.prompt: An atom has atomic number 17 and mass number 35. State the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in a neutral atom. (3)
hints: For a neutral atom, electrons equal protons.
questions.solution:
Protons = 17 because atomic number is the proton number. [B1]
Electrons = 17 because the atom is neutral. [B1]
Neutrons = 35 - 17 = 18. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the trend in reactivity down Group 1 of the periodic table. (4)
questions.solution:

Down the group the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded. [B1]
The attraction between the nucleus and outer electron is weaker. [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare the typical properties of transition metals with Group 1 metals. (4)

questions.prompt: Explain how the periodic table developed from early arrangements to the modern table. (4)

questions.prompt: Explain why ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten but not when solid. (4)
hints: Compare ion mobility in solid and liquid states.
questions.solution:
Ionic compounds contain charged ions. [B1]
In a solid lattice the ions are fixed in position and cannot move. [B1]
When molten the ions are free to move. [B1]
Moving ions carry electric charge through the liquid. [B1]
questions.inspiredBy: AQA 8462 Chemistry Paper 1 style · Bonding, structure, and the properties of matter · family 1

questions.prompt: Explain why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not. (4)
hints: How many bonds does each carbon make?
questions.solution:
Both are giant covalent forms of carbon. [B1]
In graphite each carbon forms three covalent bonds, leaving one delocalised electron per carbon. [B1]
The delocalised electrons can move and carry charge. [B1]
In diamond each carbon forms four covalent bonds so there are no free electrons or ions to carry charge. [B1]
questions.inspiredBy: AQA 8462 Chemistry Paper 1 style · Bonding, structure, and the properties of matter · family 2

questions.prompt: Explain why metals are malleable and conduct electricity. (4)
hints: Different features explain malleability and conductivity.
questions.solution:
Metals consist of positive ions in a lattice surrounded by delocalised electrons. [B1]
Layers of metal ions can slide past one another while metallic bonding is maintained, so the metal is malleable. [B1]
Delocalised electrons are free to move through the structure. [B1]
The moving electrons carry electrical charge. [B1]
questions.inspiredBy: AQA 8462 Chemistry Paper 1 style · Bonding, structure, and the properties of matter · family 3

questions.prompt: Explain why nanoparticles can have properties different from larger particles of the same material. (4)
hints: Relate small size to both benefits and risks.

questions.prompt: Compare simple molecular substances with giant covalent structures in terms of melting point. (4)

Only weak intermolecular forces need to be overcome when simple molecular substances melt, so melting points are low. [B1]
